What is true (Kooijman et al., Science 2011, https://swov.nl/en/publicatie/bicycle-can-be-self-stable-without-gyroscopic-or-caster-effects) is that neither the gyroscopic effect nor trail is necessary in principle: a specially designed 'two-mass-skate' bicycle balances with neither. On an ordinary bicycle, both contribute. The rest holds up: distinct from feedback-control, level 3 is honest (linearised multibody eigenvalues), the model is a 4x4 linear system that runs at interactive rates, and the parameters are published.

fixed.interaction: Push a riderless bicycle at a chosen speed and let its linearized equations of motion run: below a certain speed it slowly falls, in a middle band it wobbles and recovers on its own, and above it it slowly leans away. Drag the speed and watch the eigenvalues of lean and steer cross the stability boundary; change the trail, the head angle and the front-wheel mass, cancel the gyroscopic effect of the wheels and the trail in turn and see the ordinary bicycle lose its self-stable band, then load the two-mass-skate design that balances with neither; finally steer left and watch the bike first lean right.
fixed.takeaway: A riderless bicycle balances itself in a band of speeds because a lean makes its front wheel steer into the fall, and that self-steering comes from the geometry and mass of the whole front assembly, not from any single effect such as the wheels' gyroscopic spin.
fixed.pitfall: Neither 'the gyroscope keeps it up' nor 'the gyroscope plays no part' is right. On the standard benchmark bicycle, cancelling the wheels' gyroscopic effect removes its self-stable speed band. Yet Kooijman et al. (2011) built a bicycle that balances with neither a gyroscopic effect nor trail. Self-stability comes from several effects working together.

verdicts.reason: The Brayton half substantially duplicates jet-engines, a level-3 page in this same pool that already plots a gas turbine on a T-s diagram from its cycle, station by station. The only new mechanism is the coupling: the heat-recovery boiler and its pinch point, and why the pair beats either engine alone. The pitfall is also muddled. 'Over half the turbine work' is only true on average: typical back-work ratios are 40 to 80 percent (Purdue ME 200 notes, https://engineering.purdue.edu/~wassgren/teaching/ME20000/NotesAndReading/Lec39_Reading_Wassgren.pdf). fixed.interaction: Set a gas turbine's pressure ratio and turbine inlet temperature and watch its exhaust leave at several hundred degrees; then route that exhaust through a heat-recovery steam generator drawn as a temperature-heat diagram, the cooling gas line above the heating water-and-steam line. Drag the steam pressure and the pinch-point gap, add a second and third pressure level, and see the two lines hug more closely, the stack temperature fall and the plant's combined efficiency climb past 60 percent.
fixed.takeaway: A combined-cycle plant reaches about 60 percent efficiency because a steam cycle turns the gas turbine's hot exhaust into extra work, and it recovers more the more closely the steam's heating line can follow the cooling exhaust.
fixed.pitfall: The best gas turbine for a combined cycle is not the most efficient stand-alone one. A lower pressure ratio leaves a hotter exhaust for the steam cycle, so the plant's optimum pressure ratio is below the gas turbine's own. And the steam cycle burns no extra fuel: it only uses heat that would otherwise go up the stack.

Level 3 is honest: it is LLM-systems course material, and its prerequisites are L2 and L3. Buildable with a char-level target and a bigram draft over the same vocabulary. fixed.interaction: A cheap draft model guesses the next few tokens and the large target model checks them all in one pass: step through each guess, accepted with probability min(1, p/q) or rejected and replaced by a sample from the leftover distribution max(0, p - q), with p and q drawn as overlapping bar charts. When every guess is accepted, the target's own pass adds one more token for free. Change the number of guesses and swap in a better or worse draft to see the tokens gained per target pass, then run ten thousand samples and watch their histogram converge on the target model's distribution.

Accepting only exact matches with the target's top choice is valid only for greedy decoding. The speed-up pays off because a decode pass at small batch is memory-bound, so checking several tokens costs about as much as one; the tiny models on the page are not memory-bound, so the page counts target passes, not seconds.

verdicts.reason: Distinct from language-models, which only shows text split into tokens; this page builds BPE merge by merge and applies GPT-2's real merges. Level 3 is defensible: university NLP courses teach byte-level BPE, with its regex pre-split and rank-order merging, and the prerequisites are L2. Data: tiktoken is MIT, and OpenAI's gpt-2 repository and the Hugging Face openai-community/gpt2 repository (which ships vocab.json and merges.txt) carry modified-MIT and MIT licences, so it is usable. The takeaway is factually wrong (rule 5): 'never sees letters' is false. GPT-2 has single-character tokens, and rare words and byte fallback do break down to letters. What is true is that the model cannot see the letters inside a merged token. A small rewording fixes it.

fixed.takeaway: Tokens are built by greedily merging the most frequent pairs in the training text, so a model sees whole words where text is common and fragments where it is rare, and cannot see the letters inside a token.
fixed.pitfall: Merges apply in rank order, not by longest match, so the split is deterministic given the merge list; byte-level BPE never needs an unknown token. Do not say models never see letters (single characters are tokens too), nor that they count letters: inside a merged token the spelling is invisible to them.

verdicts.reason: Distinct and honest at L3: it is the 'Let's build GPT' material, the existing language-models page only reads precomputed probabilities, and the prerequisites are L2 and proposed L1 and L3. Rule 3 risk as written: training to convergence live in the browser for every width, context and data setting is minutes of compute per point, and no browser demo of live transformer training turned up (the TF.js example is an LSTM and warns that browser training is slow). Promising that it beats the 5-gram line is unsafe. A two-layer model with tens of thousands of weights may not beat a well-smoothed char 5-gram within a short browser run, and an unsmoothed 5-gram scores badly on validation, so the line depends on smoothing. Also, 'a fixed order' of sample improvement is an observed tendency, not a law. Fix: train only the default configuration live, in a Web Worker with a fixed seed, ship precomputed curves and samples for the parameter grid, and commit only to the bigram and smoothed trigram lines.

fixed.takeaway: Training a language model is gradient descent on one number, the average surprise at the next character, and as that number falls the samples go from random letters to plausible spelling to words and line structure.

The order in which samples improve is a typical pattern, not a guaranteed sequence.
